candidate.messageText:
🛠 ۵ ابزار که کلاد رو توی پروژه‌ت مثل یه senior developer می‌کنه

1️⃣ اسکیل Fullstack Dev Skills
یه پک کامل از skillها، از frontend و backend تا test و deploy. لازم نیست انتخاب کنی؛ کلاد بسته به کاری که بهش می‌دی، skill مناسبش رو خودش برمی‌داره.
🔗 github.com/jeffallan/claude-skills
نصب توی Claude Code:
/plugin marketplace add jeffallan/claude-skills
/plugin install fullstack-dev-skills@fullstack-dev-skills

2️⃣ اسکیل Context7
آخرین documentation کتابخونه‌ای که باهاش کار می‌کنی رو میاره جلوی کلاد، تا با اطلاعات نسخه‌های قدیمی برات کد نزنه.
🔗 github.com/upstash/context7

3️⃣ اسکیل Graphify
از کد پروژه‌ت یه نقشه (knowledge graph) می‌سازه که کلاد بفهمه هر فایل و هر تابع به کجا وصله. این‌جوری قبل از هر تغییر می‌دونه روی کجاهای دیگه اثر می‌ذاره.
🔗 github.com/safishamsi/graphify

4️⃣ اسکیل Magic MCP از 21st.dev
به کلاد دسترسی می‌ده به کلی component آماده، که با یه دستور بذارتشون توی پروژه‌ت.
🔗 github.com/21st-dev/magic-mcp

5️⃣ اسکیل vibe-check
وقتی با vibe coding یه چیزی ساختی، قبل از انتشار کد رو بررسی می‌کنه، ایرادای امنیتی و چیزایی که جا موندن رو پیدا می‌کنه و کمک می‌کنه درستشون کنی.
🔗 github.com/vibe-safety/vibe-check
نصب توی Claude Code:
/plugin marketplace add 
/plugin install vibe-check@vibe-safety

@mgh_mobin

Meta won’t force Facebook page owners to allow AI training on linked content.
After weeks of backlash —and a failed attempt to quell it —Meta has indefinitely delayed plans to update its commercial terms and require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.
“We’re pausing the ‌changes ⁠as we continue to engage with stakeholders and ​take ​our ⁠time to get this right. ​In the ​meantime, ⁠our existing terms remain in ⁠effect,” a Meta spokesperson told Reuters.
Soon after Meta notified business account holders of the upcoming changes, legal experts warned Nieman Lab that the vague language could allow the company to ignore scraping preferences specified in robots.txt files and exhaustively crawl vast amounts of off-Facebook content for AI training. Since virtually every news publisher has a Facebook page, Nieman Lab sounded the alarm that Meta could potentially avoid millions in licensing fees if the TOS update happened as planned.
Ars broke down the changes after Meta announced them, noting that businesses—including news publishers involved in drawn-out legal battles over unwanted AI scraping—had no way to opt out. To keep a business Facebook page, they had to allow Meta to crawl any linked external sites. In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

A former Rockstar tech director thinks the developer is facing new time pressures.
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.

Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. published.sourceText:
Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a coding-agent benchmark from real user change requests. Even the best model fully completes only about one in four tasks, putting the near-perfect scores of older tests into perspective.
The team developed Co-Design Bench, a new test for coding agents. The agents must rework existing web apps based on user requests, sometimes using images, audio recordings, videos, or documents as input.
According to the paper, GPT-6 Astra, the best of the ten models tested, meets about 70 percent of a task's requirements on average. But the result is fully correct in only 26.4 percent of tasks. In most cases the agent handles the bulk of the work but leaves at least one detail unfinished, so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand.

Coding benchmarks have grown too easy for agents
The authors justify the new test by pointing to the saturation of existing benchmarks. When models can run, check, and fix their own code, they hit scores above 99 percent on those tests, and differences between models can barely be measured.

If you were in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, today’s AI boom might feel familiar. In 1998 and 1999, internet traffic was roughly doubling every six to nine months. That was extraordinary growth in demand, and still, that pales in comparison to what we’re seeing unfold now.
Today, the four largest U.S. cloud companies are looking at more than $700 billion in capital spending this year, and the cumulative AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030.
Nvidia arguably fired the starting gun in AI chips when Jensen Huang hand-delivered its DGX-1 to OpenAI in 2016. Today, it is a household name deeply embedded in the AI ecosystem, working with near-exclusive supply and investment deals.
With such a huge market under a seeming monopoly, where can competition — and the innovation that follows it — come from?
Part of the answer is that scale costs you speed, though when going up against an execution machine like Nvidia this is simply the baseline you have to solve for. The pace of change in AI outruns anything we saw in previous tech cycles: Model generations turn over in weeks, not years. Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb.
It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!
I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

published.sourceText:
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

published.sourceText:
Hackers allegedly assisted by AI breached a German web hosting company through a tool designed to allow customers to connect AI assistants to their accounts, the company disclosed over the weekend.
Mittwald CM Service, a hosting provider for web agencies based in North Rhine-Westphalia, disclosed in a blog post Saturday that hackers had compromised 56 customer projects after going undetected on its systems for eight days.
The company’s managing director Robert Meyer said the attackers exploited a flaw in Mittwald’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server used to allow customers to connect their AI assistants to mStudio, a platform for managing websites and hosting services. It is unclear whether the flaw was in the company’s own code or in the open-source MCP software libraries.
Meyer said the attacker appeared to have used AI tools in the breach, explaining the company’s logs “show that he worked his way through our system extremely quickly” and that “in some cases, only seconds passed between steps that would take significantly longer for a human attacker.”
Mittwald provided no other evidence of AI involvement. The company did not immediately respond when asked to distinguish between the detection of AI tools and conventional scripts that also allow hackers to move faster than an unaided human operator.

published.sourceTitle: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
published.sourceText:
“Do not ask again” prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. published.sourceTitle: Andrej Karpathy built a curated video platform in a weekend using Claude and 20 years of Hacker News
published.sourceText:
Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI co-founder and current Anthropic AI researcher, built HackerTube over a weekend using Claude's Opus 5.5 model. Claude filtered 43 million comments from 20 years of Hacker News and distilled them into 6,454 videos that keep getting recommended there . The result is a "significantly better viewing experience" than YouTube's own recommendations, Karpathy writes on X . The site needs no login, shows a single mid-video frame instead of optimized thumbnails, and stores state locally in the browser. Right after, Karpathy built TristanTube , "one-shotted with Claude Code in 3 minutes," with 47,000 videos drawn from a YouTube channel list by Tristan Hume.
Karpathy says he let Claude Code handle nearly all the work, from data analysis to server setup. His only manual steps were a Google Cloud API key, a rented server, and buying the domain. Projects that used to take weeks can now be done in a few hours, Karpathy says.
